card.title: Colligative properties — counting particles, not kinds

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Dissolved particles lower the solvent's escaping tendency (vapour pressure drops by mole fraction — Raoult), so boiling needs more heat (ΔTb) and freezing comes easier (ΔTf); across a semipermeable membrane the same pull is osmotic pressure π = CRT. All four depend on particle COUNT, never identity — electrolytes multiply the effect by the van't Hoff factor i (dissociation) or shrink it (association).

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: Raoult: P = x_solvent·P° · ΔP/P° = x_solute  ·  ΔTb = i·Kb·m · ΔTf = i·Kf·m · π = iCRT  ·  i = observed/calculated (NaCl → ~2, CaCl₂ → ~3, acetic-acid dimer → ~0.5)  ·  concentration: M, m, %w/w, ppm, mole fraction

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Colligative laws need dilute, non-volatile-solute solutions (solute must not join the vapour). Molality (not molarity) for ΔT laws — temperature-independent. van't Hoff corrections assume ideal dissociation/association equilibria; ion pairing at high concentration breaks ideality.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NaCl: i ≈ 2 doubles every effect (abnormal molar mass halves). Acetic acid dimerises in benzene: i ≈ 0.5, apparent mass doubles. Reverse osmosis desalinates against π with pressure. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) and road salt are ΔTf applications; IV fluids match blood π (~0.9% NaCl isotonic).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Molar mass from ΔTf: dissolve w₂ grams in w₁ kg solvent, measure depression ΔTf → M₂ = (i·Kf·w₂)/(ΔTf·w₁). With association (benzoic acid in benzene), the computed mass doubles — the abnormality that reveals dimerisation. Same ladder climbs ΔTb and π.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Colligative laws fail concentrated solutions (activity replaces concentration) and volatile solutes (both components join vapour — fractional distillation territory). van't Hoff i is empirical per condition, not a molecular constant. Osmosis needs truly semipermeable membranes.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Raoult from escaping tendency: each surface molecule is solvent with probability x_solvent → P = x·P°. Chemical-potential equality (μ_liquid = μ_vapour) then forces boiling-point rise and freezing-point drop proportional to solute mole fraction; dilute-limit expansion gives ΔT = K·m with solvent constants Kb, Kf. Electrolytes: count the actual particles — i.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: 'Abnormal molar mass' → write i first (dissociate >1, associate <1). ΔT laws: molality always. Osmosis: π = CRT with T in kelvin. Concentration conversions: M↔m needs density; mole fraction needs no density.
